dedupe_keys.name: global analysis which national food system capacities decouple undernourishment from shocks

description: This case study analyses why some countries' food systems keep food insecurity from rising when hit by climate extremes, conflict, pandemics or economic shocks. The authors, led by Christophe Béné of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT with colleagues from CIRAD, Cornell University, City St George's University of London, the European Commission, the Food and Agriculture Organization and others, built a multi-country dataset combining shock severity, governance, economic conditions, social capital and food system characteristics, and used a causal resilience-as-capacity framework with hybrid econometric models to explain changes in the prevalence of undernourishment. The article was published in PNAS in September 2026 and is free to read online under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives licence. Coverage is global, by country. Caveats: national indicators hide within-country differences, and undernourishment is a slow-moving estimate. More severe shocks did not systematically lead to worse food security, and several highly affected countries, particularly in Asia, did well; countries with stronger resilience capacities and more favourable food system characteristics fared better, with improvements in government effectiveness, food supply redundancy or GDP per capita reducing deterioration and stronger social capital supporting long-term gains. Simulation uses: evidence on capacities that buffer food supply shocks, for national resilience and scenario models. Related records: the DARTS food system model (model-darts-food-system) and the Global Food Security Projections Database (data-global-food-security-projections-database) model related outcomes.
